2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern / Can't tell: Data collection consisted of single-timepoint semi-structured interviews; however, initial recruitment refusal/non-response rates (including during the two-month COVID-19 inter-district travel ban) are not reported, and high local government turnover plus COVID-19 restrictions prevented full post-interview participant validation (PDF pp. 8, 19).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design with no quantitative causal effect estimation). Contextually, all 3 sampled districts already had active Area Service Providers for several years and interviews took place in the year preceding Uganda's national elections, both of which shaped observed political and institutional dynamics as acknowledged by the authors (PDF pp. 7, 13, 19).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: High / Strong for qualitative institutional research: The authors systematically compiled, vetted, and coded 9 Ugandan statutes, national policies, and implementation manuals from 1997 to 2019 in QSR NVivo 12—including The Water Act (1997), The Local Governments Act (1997), the 2004 O&M Framework, and the 2019 National Framework for Operation and Maintenance of Rural Water Infrastructure in Uganda—clearly mapping de jure district and sub-county mandates against de facto fiscal and political practices (PDF pp. 6-7, 10, Table 1).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: Interviews followed tailored semi-structured guides (S1 File), were conducted in English by two trained Ugandan research assistants with no prior exposure to service providers or respondents, and were deductively double-coded by two independent coders with good inter-coder agreement (Cohen's Kappa = 0.78; PDF p. 8). However, self-reported accounts of informal campaign borehole financing, 'facilitation' payments, and statutory compliance remain vulnerable to social desirability bias, full member-checking was not possible (PDF p. 19), and the role of Whave Solutions co-authors and field staff in interview guide input and validation was not critically examined (PDF pp. 2, 21).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / Perceptual only: The study rigorously categorizes local government support behaviors across the Service Delivery Cycle (construction, rehabilitation, O&M, administration/management, direct support, and indirect support) using double-coded interview transcripts (PDF pp. 8-17), but measures only self-reported institutional support actions and perceptions rather than objective physical borehole functionality, repair speed, water quality, or verified tariff collection outcomes.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low concern: The authors transparently report full coding definitions (S1 Table), frequency matrices across all regulative, normative, cultural-cognitive, and 'other' categories (Table 3; S2-S5 Tables), the complete interview guide (S1 File), and divergent/negative accounts across both political and technical officials, while appropriately withholding raw transcripts under IRB confidentiality rules (PDF pp. 1-2, 8-17, 20-21).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: Although the sample of 93 local government actors is balanced across political (47) and technical (46) roles across 22 sub-counties in 3 districts (PDF p. 7, Table 2), the paper does not report how districts, sub-counties, or individual respondents were selected, how many invited officials declined, or how assistance from Whave Solutions field staff during 'research setup and fieldwork' (PDF p. 21) shaped selection within the 3 districts where Whave Solutions operates (PDF pp. 2, 19).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors clearly state the study's purpose—examining shifts in local government roles under Uganda's 2019 National O&M Framework and identifying regulative, normative, and cultural-cognitive influences on their fulfillment—and pose two explicit research questions grounded in rural water sustainability and decentralization literature.

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative methodology (qualitative policy document coding paired with semi-structured interviews analyzed through Organizational Institutional Theory) is well suited to uncovering taken-for-granted cultural-cognitive beliefs, social norms, political expectations, and subjective role interpretations of local government actors.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining qualitative coding of 9 Ugandan statutory and policy texts (1997-2019) to establish formal mandate shifts with 93 semi-structured interviews spanning both elected political (47) and appointed technical (46) officials at district and sub-county tiers directly addresses how formal policy interacts with informal institutional pillars.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6-8 (Methods > Policy comparison; Interview data collection; Table 1; Table 2)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: While Table 2 clearly documents the composition of the 93 interviewees across technical/political roles and district/sub-county tiers in 22 sub-counties across 3 districts with active Area Service Providers, the paper does not explain how the 3 districts, 22 sub-counties, or individual officials were sampled, whether any invited officials declined to participate, or what role Whave Solutions field staff played in participant selection during 'research setup and fieldwork.'
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF p. 7 (Methods > Interview data collection; Table 2); PDF p. 19 (Discussion); PDF p. 21 (Acknowledgments)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection procedures are explicitly justified and detailed: semi-structured interview guides tailored to technical and political actors (provided in S1 File, with sample questions in text), 45-90 minute interviews conducted in English by trained Ugandan research assistants, audio recording and transcription totaling 3,380 minutes (with detailed notes for 2 unrecorded respondents), and documented COVID-19 fieldwork pause and safety protocols.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 7-8 (Methods > Interview data collection; Interview data analysis)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors took an explicit step to mitigate direct interviewer bias by hiring two Ugandan research assistants with no prior exposure to service providers or study participants (PDF p. 8) and disclosed in Competing Interests that two co-authors (AH, EB) are employed by Whave Solutions, an Area Service Provider operating in all three study districts (PDF p. 2). However, the paper does not critically examine how selecting the three districts where Whave Solutions operates, receiving input on interview guides and 'assistance during research setup and fieldwork' from Whave Solutions field staff, and having Whave co-authors perform 'Investigation' and 'Validation' (PDF p. 21) may have influenced recruitment, perceived affiliation, or analytical interpretation.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF p. 2 (Competing interests); PDF p. 8 (Methods > Interview data collection); PDF p. 21 (Acknowledgments; Author Contributions)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Ethical procedures are thoroughly documented, including University of Colorado Boulder IRB approval (protocol #19-0605), an IRB-approved waiver of written consent with documented verbal informed consent, permission from each district's Chief Administrative Officer, strict de-identification of excerpts and metadata to protect local officials, and COVID-19 protective measures.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1-2 (Data Availability Statement); PDF pp. 8-10 (Methods > Interview data collection; Ethics statement)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative analysis is systematic and transparent: 3,380 minutes of transcripts were deductively double-coded in QSR NVivo 12 across two conceptual sub-structures (Service Delivery Cycle and Organizational Institutional Theory) by two independent coders who refined definitions (S1 Table) and achieved Cohen's Kappa = 0.78, applied explicit filtering rules for cross-group claims, and supported findings with rich verbatim quotes and frequency matrices (Table 3, S2-S5 Tables).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 8-9 (Methods > Interview data analysis; Fig 4); PDF pp. 10-17 (Results; Table 3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly structured around formal policy shifts and Service Delivery Cycle support stages, systematically contrast technical vs. political and district vs. sub-county actors, highlight divergent supportive and unsupportive enactments of the same institutional norms, and explicitly discuss credibility and transferability limitations (including restriction to 3 districts with prior ASP presence and inability to complete full participant validation).

High research value (narrative assessment): The study provides timely empirical insight into why formal national policy reform (Uganda's 2019 O&M Framework) is insufficient on its own to secure local government service-authority support without aligning mandates with local normative expectations, political leader identities, and central-to-local fiscal transfers, while clearly identifying future research needs in districts without prior ASP exposure.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable (high empirical and policy relevance; narrative assessment)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Cord et al. (2022) is a primary qualitative study combining qualitative documentary analysis of 9 Ugandan water and decentralization laws/policies (1997-2019) with semi-structured interviews of 93 district and sub-county technical (46) and political (47) local government actors across 22 sub-counties in 3 Ugandan districts. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study demonstrates low-to-moderate methodological concern (7 'Yes', 2 'Can't tell', 0 'No' on Q1-Q9, and high value on Q10). Strengths include clearly articulated research questions grounded in Organizational Institutional Theory and the Service Delivery Cycle, comprehensive coding of Uganda's statutory and policy framework, large and balanced interview coverage of both elected and appointed local officials, independent Ugandan interviewers, rigorous double-coding in NVivo 12 with documented inter-coder agreement (Cohen's Kappa = 0.78), thorough IRB and confidentiality safeguards, and nuanced reporting of divergent perspectives. The two 'Can't tell' ratings reflect (1) incomplete reporting of sampling/recruitment mechanics and non-response rates across the 3 districts and 22 sub-counties (Q4), and (2) partial reflexivity (Q6): although independent local research assistants conducted the interviews and co-authors' employment with Whave Solutions (an Area Service Provider active in all three study districts) was disclosed, the authors did not critically examine how Whave Solutions co-authors and field staff assisting with interview guide design, research setup, fieldwork, and validation may have shaped participant selection or interpretation, alongside the absence of objective physical water-point outcome data.
raw_response.overall_rating: Low-to-moderate methodological concern (7 Yes, 2 Can't tell, 0 No across Q1-Q9; high research value on Q10)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative study (qualitative documentary coding of 9 Ugandan laws/policies paired with 93 semi-structured interviews of local government technical and political actors)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract & Data Availability Statement (PDF pp. 1-2); Funding & Competing Interests (PDF p. 2); Study Aims & Theoretical Overview (PDF pp. 2-6); Methods: Policy Comparison, Interview Data Collection, Interview Data Analysis, Ethics Statement (PDF pp. 6-10, Tables 1-2, Fig 4); Results (PDF pp. 10-17, Table 3, Fig 5); Discussion & Limitations (PDF pp. 17-19); Conclusions, Supporting Information, Acknowledgments & Author Contributions (PDF pp. 19-21).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper explicitly states that 'Only qualitative data was used for this study' (PDF p. 1) and employs qualitative coding of 9 legal/policy texts alongside 93 semi-structured interviews analyzed deductively in QSR NVivo 12. Descriptive relative frequencies of coded excerpts in Table 3 summarize qualitative coding matrices rather than constituting a separate quantitative survey or econometric component; therefore, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching appraisal instrument rather than MMAT or JBI Cross-Sectional.
